doc.title: Slide Hampton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Showmanship: Armstrong, Cab Calloway and Hamp's ego
summary: Hampton traces Hamp's showmanship to Armstrong, discusses Cab Calloway, and says ego distracted Hamp.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Do you think that’s because he was straddling an era? He came from an era when it was about showmen, and transitioned into an era where another kind of consciousness came into the music. He goes back to the ’20s. He probably – excluding Louis Armstrong, he had probably one of the longest expanses stylistically and in time, in the music.

That’s true. He did come from an area where entertainment was very important. Louis Armstrong was one of the great examples. Of course a lot of people don’t realize that, along with all of that entertainment, there was a hell of a lot of genius going on. That probably distracted people sometimes from seeing really what he was doing, because he was such a great entertainer. So Lionel Hampton probably was influenced by Louis Armstrong in this entertainment area of music. Louis Armstrong had a big success with this stuff. He probably – a lot of the guys that came not too long after that felt as though you had to do that. Even up to the bebop period, when Dizzy started his band, he was still being influenced by that thing with Louis Armstrong, entertaining.
And Cab Calloway. That’s a band I didn’t ask you about. Did that figure in your calculus at all?
Of course, because Dizzy played with him, and a lot of other good guys played with him.
So that’s a part of that time of the intersecting bands, and these guys jump from this band to that band.

They were influenced by Cab, because Cab Calloway had some really good bands. What they didn’t like is, they didn’t really like all the showmanship that he was using all the time. But he did that. That was him. It was natural for him. But Dizzy and them didn’t like it. So sometimes when they were in the band, they’d be doing things like – he’d be out there going, “Hi de hi de ho,” and they’d be throwing things and hitting him on the back of the head. At the same token, they learned a lot about entertainment from that guy.
Even as they made fun of it.
Even as they made – and then when they went into their bands, they used that experience.
Used some of the same things. It sounds like you liked playing in the Hampton band, but you might have found his leadership problematic.

What I found was what he could have accomplished was somewhat hindered by his, “I want to be in the spotlight all the time.” Distractions. Those are distractions that we all could have. Distractions are everywhere just waiting. Every corner you turn around, there’s some distractions waiting for you, and if you don’t keep going, they’ll get you. He was distracted all the time by his ego. But he was the guy that was always trying to learn. He was always playing the vibes, and he was listening to the other guys, playing and say, “Come on, Gates. Play this with me.” He was always trying to learn, but he had this other thing that was distracting him.
